panels.figure_caption: The four viability signs. Videos were taken with a handheld digital video microscope with a 5 mega-pixel optical resolution. (A) Expulsion of eggs, (B) excretion of fecal thread, (C) excretion of fecal liquid, and (D) pulsations/contractions. For (D), the color of the surrounding skin changed rhythmically with the beating of the pulse. Also, it is possible to see the external, moving abdominal cone.
in_text_mentions: The primary endpoint was the cure rate (proportion of dead fleas) on day 7 after treatment with either 5% sodium carbonate solution or NYDA. Embedded fleas were assessed using a digital handheld microscope at baseline and on days 3, 5, and 7 for the following four signs of viability: expulsion of eggs, excretion of fecal threads, excretion of fecal liquid, and pulsations/contractions (Fig 1).
Moreover, 20 fleas (NYDA: 10 fleas; 5% sodium carbonate: 10 fleas) were excluded from the analysis (Fig 1), because we did not know whether they died or were removed by someone else.

panels.rationale: Single dermoscopic image of a human plantar tungiasis lesion. The caption and in-text mentions explicitly attribute the findings to tungiasis: a central brown crateriform structure with a peripheral yellowish halo and pigmented ring (embedded flea) plus clustered whitish ovoid parasite eggs on adjacent plantar skin. These are textbook dermoscopic features of tungiasis, so the panel is included with high confidence. No ethnicity or patient age is stated for this figure.

panels.figure_caption: Dermoscopic appearance of a tungiasis lesion. A central brown crateriform structure is visible, surrounded by a peripheral yellowish halo and a distinct pigmented ring. Several parasite eggs are attached to the adjacent plantar skin surface.
in_text_mentions: Dermoscopy consistently revealed a central brown crateriform structure surrounded by a peripheral yellowish halo and a distinct pigmented ring. In several lesions, multiple whitish ovoid structures corresponding to parasite eggs were identified, further supporting the clinical diagnosis of tungiasis (Figure 2). Notably, in patients who had been wearing socks prior to clinical evaluation, a more pronounced accumulation of parasite eggs on the skin surface of the feet was observed. In our clinical experience, this finding facilitated both suspicion and confirmation of the diagnosis.

in_text_mentions: In total, 252 (42.5%) individuals were infested with T. penetrans. Of these, 122 (48.4%) presented with mild, 105 (41.7%) with moderate, and 25 (9.9%) with heavy infestation. The age-specific prevalences and intensities of infestation are shown in Figure 1. Prevalence followed an S-shaped pattern and was highest in children 5 to 9 years of age, 10 to 15-years old adolescents and the elderly. The highest proportion of individuals with heavy infestation was observed in the elderly.

By consequence, rather large areas of the skin are exposed to sand fleas which, in turn, explains the high parasite burden and the ectopic localizations (Figs 1B, 1C, 2B and 3B) [41, 42]. in_text_mentions: All eight patients, including seven men with recent travel history to Tanzania and one non-traveling household contact, presented with painful plantar and/or subungual nodular lesions. The patients commonly reported moderate pruritus and a sensation of a foreign body in the affected area. Clinically, the lesions were typically yellowish and characterized by a central dark punctum surrounded by a mildly erythematous halo (Figure 1A–C). No lower limb edema or regional lymph node enlargement was detected during clinical examination.

In the non-traveling household contact, a single lesion was identified in the subungual region of the second toe of the left foot (Figure 1C). The absence of travel history, together with compatible clinical and dermoscopic findings, suggests probable secondary household transmission.

in_text_mentions: ase caused by the female sand flea Tunga penetrans (Siphonaptera), which is native to South America [1]. panels.rationale: H&E histopathology of an excised human tongue lesion from a case report titled 'Tungiasis presenting as a soft tissue oral lesion.' The image shows the chitinous exoskeleton of the sand flea enclosing compartments packed with ova (eggs), bordered by neutrophilic, macrophage and giant-cell inflammatory infiltrate, and the in-text diagnosis confirms 'tungiasis of the tongue.' This is a real patient tissue image with a specific diagnostic manifestation of tungiasis (gravid female flea with eggs), so it qualifies for the library. The tongue (oral) site is a recognized but less common presentation, hence variant typicality. No ethnicity or age is stated in the caption or in-text mentions.

in_text_mentions: acrophages and giant cells, some lymphocytes and occasional eosinophils. Several oval-shaped structures, some intact some cracked, aggregated in compartments that occupied most of the space. Discontinuous spiral-bound elongations at the periphery of the lesion represented the flea’s chitinous exoskeleton (Figures 2, 3 and 4). Based on the circular containment of numerous oval aggregations, elongated fractionated segments encapsulating the space and accumulation at the tissue-lesion interface of inflammatory cells characteristic of a foreign body reaction, tungiasis of the tongue was diagnosed.

panels.rationale: Single H&E histology image (X20) of a human tongue lesion showing numerous cracked ova (E) and the flea's rigid epicuticle/chitinous exoskeleton (F) within tissue, accompanied by a foreign-body inflammatory reaction. Tongue (oral) involvement is a recognized but less common presentation, hence variant; Fitzpatrick tone is not assessable from a tissue section.
